title: The Problem
subtitle: Spoofed caller IDs, lost trust and a regulatory gap: why today’s all-IP telephone network cannot protect the people who use it.
endNote: Next: how PSTN2 solves this, without a central database.

scenes.title: A network people no longer trust

segments.text: Today’s public telephone network is highly vulnerable.
The move to all-IP did not come with matching safeguards, and the network now struggles against modern threats.
Fraud losses are estimated at $38bn a year.
segments.say: Fraud losses are estimated at thirty-eight billion dollars a year.

segments.text: Trust in what was once the most trusted network has fallen so far that people have stopped answering the phone.
That is a threat to the industry, and to the wider economy.
Fraudsters thrive, because they face almost no risk of being caught.
Spoofing a caller ID is technically trivial. The screen shows whatever name and number the fraudster chooses.
Victims trust what their phone tells them, and some see their lives destroyed.
As the public learns how easy spoofing is, the historic trust in the telephone network keeps eroding.
Industry effort goes into regulatory compliance, rather than into advancing privacy, security and consumer protection.
When consumers are harmed, the sector’s long-term credibility is weakened.
The industry must work with regulators to restore trust in the network, while letting innovation flourish safely.
In the all-IP era, the greatest gains have gone to social networks and over-the-top messaging platforms.
Not to the industry that built the internet, still maintains it, and should have benefited.
All-IP has outpaced regulation, leaving critical gaps that allow criminal activity on a large scale.
To protect consumers and the integrity of communications, regulators must act against this existential threat.
Mandatory technical safeguards are needed: safeguards that recognise the shift from physical to digital sources of truth, and keep pace with the threat.
And the pace of change driven by artificial intelligence makes action more urgent than ever.
Take the proposal for a central numbering database, now recognised as a key enabler for many of today’s challenges.
It was estimated at around £2m to build, and around £600k a year to run: thirty percent of the build cost, every year.
Industry raised economic, technical and time-to-value concerns, and the proposal was not progressed.
One-Touch Switch raised similar concerns. But it went ahead, because the regulator mandated it.
Future innovations may need the same regulatory push.
The industry lacks effective tools to prevent fraud, and essential safeguards for all-IP are missing from regulatory policy.
An assertive regulatory strategy for the all-IP network is needed, to keep it commercially viable and trusted by consumers.
All-IP should have unlocked real innovation for the only global public communications network. Treating it as a mere back-end replacement has stifled that.
Regulation needs a policy shift: from competition through switching, to competition through innovation that takes advantage of all-IP.
But what if there were another way?
What if we could deliver all of these capabilities without a central database?
Without big-bang changes, and without investment that cannot be justified?
Without waiting for everyone to agree? And perhaps, without waiting for the regulator to acquire the latest technology skills?
Introducing PSTN2.
PSTN2 is a set of free-to-use software libraries and documentation.
It lets providers add privacy and security to their customers’ calls with every other PSTN2 participant.
At last, it adds value back into person-to-person communication, instead of joining the race to the bottom on commodity pricing.
